title: Juniper JNCIA-Junos (JN0-106) Study Guide
description: JNCIA-Junos (JN0-106) is the associate-level certification for the Junos operating system and the baseline for both the Enterprise and the Service Provider routing and switching tracks. The exam is 65 multiple-choice questions in 90 minutes, English only, pass/fail with an immediate result. It covers networking fundamentals, Junos OS architecture, the CLI and user interfaces, configuration basics, operational monitoring and maintenance, routing fundamentals, and routing policy and firewall filters. Note the branding: Juniper is now part of HPE and the material is published as HPE Juniper Networking.
audience: Network engineers and technicians working on Juniper gear, Cisco-trained people who have inherited a Junos estate, and service provider staff for whom Junos is the house operating system. Beginner-to-intermediate networking knowledge is assumed — subnetting, routing and switching concepts — but there is no prerequisite certification and no required training.
why_get_it: Two honest reasons. First, the economics: complete Juniper's free Open Learning path, pass the assessment, and the $200 exam drops to $50 — no other respected vendor cert comes close to that entry price. Second, the engineering: the Junos configuration model (candidate configs, commit/rollback) teaches disciplined change management that many engineers consider saner than IOS, and it genuinely makes you better at networking regardless of vendor. In Junos-heavy environments — ISPs, carriers, service providers — this cert is the recognized front door, and Juniper skills carry a scarcity premium at the higher tiers precisely because fewer people hold them.
when_to_get_it: Take JNCIA-Junos if you touch Juniper equipment, or want to: it is common in service providers, data centres and some large enterprises, and the free training and discount make it the cheapest real networking certification going. The route is unusually good value — complete the free Open Learning course, pass the Voucher Assessment Test at 70% or better, and you get 75% off the exam, bringing $200 down to $50. The voucher expires 30 days after issue with no extension, so earn it only once you are ready to book. If your market is Cisco-dominated, CCNA is the more portable credential; JNCIA is the one that matters where Junos runs, and there is no reason not to do both when one of them is nearly free.
salary_note: Nobody publishes salary data for JNCIA specifically — an associate cert doesn't set your pay, the role does. Junior network engineer ranges run roughly $54K–$71K across major salary trackers, with BLS putting mid-career Network and Computer Systems Administrators at $96,800 median (May 2024, ~4% projected decline — openings come from replacement). Our Network Administrator path cites a lower $40–62K entry band — that's the NOC/support tier under a different BLS series; the junior market genuinely spans both. Where Juniper skills genuinely pay is upstream: JNCIS/JNCIP-level engineers in service-provider shops command a scarcity premium over equivalent Cisco tiers.
exam_format: 65 multiple-choice questions in 90 minutes via Pearson VUE (test centre or OnVUE online proctored), based on Junos OS 21.2. English only, no prerequisite certification, pass/fail with the result shown immediately. Juniper does not publish the passing score; community reports put it around 65–70%. No lab simulations.
recertification_note: Juniper certifications are valid for three years. Recertify by re-passing the current exam, or — the route most people take — by passing any higher-level exam in the track, which renews everything beneath it. No annual fees and no continuing-education bookkeeping.

items: OSI and TCP/IP models, addressing, and subnetting applied
Junos OS architecture: control plane vs forwarding plane
Transit vs exception traffic
The FreeBSD-based Junos kernel and daemon model
Junos device families and where each runs
Operational vs configuration CLI modes
The candidate configuration model: commit, commit confirmed, rollback
Configuration hierarchy, navigation, and templates
Initial device setup: users, authentication, management access
J-Web interface basics
Routing tables, route preference, and route selection
Static routing and the routing-instance concept
Dynamic routing protocol concepts (OSPF/BGP awareness level)
Routing policy: import and export controls
Firewall filters (Junos ACLs) and their evaluation order
show/monitor commands and interpreting operational output
Interface configuration and troubleshooting
System logging, tracing, and core troubleshooting workflow
Software upgrades and rescue configurations
Ping, traceroute, and reachability verification in Junos

study_steps.title: Verify you're studying for JN0-106
study_steps.description: The exam code changed in April 2026 — JN0-106 replaced JN0-105, and plenty of course listings still say the old code. Content overlap is high, but check anything you buy or watch against the current JN0-106 objectives on Juniper's site.

study_steps.title: Enroll in Juniper Open Learning — it's free and it's the whole strategy
study_steps.description: Juniper's official self-paced JNCIA-Junos courseware is free, and completing it unlocks the Voucher Assessment Test: score 70%+ (three attempts max) and you get a 75%-off voucher, making the exam $50. There is almost no excuse to pay the full $200.

study_steps.title: Shore up TCP/IP fundamentals as needed
study_steps.description: The exam assumes you can subnet and reason about basic routing before Junos specifics. If Network+-level material is shaky, patch it now — the Junos-specific content lands much easier on solid fundamentals.

study_steps.title: Get real CLI time in Juniper vLabs
study_steps.description: vLabs is free: reserve browser-based topologies with real vMX/vSRX instances — no home lab, no licenses. Practice the loop that defines Junos: edit the candidate config, commit confirmed, verify, rollback. The exam expects genuine CLI familiarity even though it's multiple choice.

study_steps.title: Read the free Day One books
study_steps.description: Juniper's free Day One PDF library — especially 'Exploring the Junos CLI' — maps almost directly onto the exam objectives and is better written than most paid books. Free, official, and exam-relevant is a rare combination; use it.

study_steps.title: Add a structured course if you want one
study_steps.description: Open Learning plus vLabs plus Day One covers most people. If you prefer a single guided video course, the well-rated Udemy options run $15–25 on sale — just confirm JN0-106 coverage before buying.

study_steps.title: Time the voucher assessment deliberately
study_steps.description: The 75%-off voucher expires 30 days after issue with no extensions — you must schedule AND sit the exam inside that window. So finish studying first, then take the Voucher Assessment Test, then book Pearson VUE immediately. Don't burn the voucher early.

study_steps.title: Sit the exam, then plan the next rung
study_steps.description: 90 minutes, 65 questions — pace is generous if you know the material. Afterward, JNCIA-Junos is rarely terminal: it gates the JNCIS tracks (Enterprise R&S, Service Provider, Security, and more), and passing a JNCIS later auto-renews this cert.

faq.question: JNCIA-Junos or CCNA — which should I get first?
faq.answer: Honestly: CCNA for general employability — it appears in vastly more U.S. job postings and is stronger HR-filter currency. Pick JNCIA-Junos first if you're targeting an ISP, carrier, or service-provider shop where Junos dominates. And for CCNA holders, JNCIA is the obvious second cert: nearly free via the voucher, fast, and it proves you're not a one-vendor engineer.

faq.question: Is the exam really only $50?
faq.answer: Effectively, yes — if you use the system as designed. Juniper Open Learning's official courseware is free; complete it, score 70%+ on the Voucher Assessment Test (three attempts max), and you receive a 75%-off Pearson VUE voucher, turning $200 into $50. The catch: the voucher expires 30 days after issue, so don't take the assessment until you're genuinely ready to book and sit the exam.

faq.question: Did the exam code change?
faq.answer: Yes — JN0-106 went live April 5, 2026, replacing JN0-105. Existing JN0-105 certs stay valid for their full 3-year term. Watch for stale study material: plenty of popular courses still say JN0-105 in the title. Content overlap is high, but verify against the current objectives.

faq.question: Is JNCIA-Junos easier than CCNA?
faq.answer: Generally yes — it's shorter (65 questions, 90 minutes), pure multiple choice with no lab sims, and more focused in scope. That's also its honest weakness: it's passable by memorization, which is exactly why hiring managers weight hands-on stories (vLabs, home lab, real tickets) over the paper. Do the labs anyway; the commit/rollback workflow is the actual career value.

faq.question: What's the deal with Juniper and HPE?
faq.answer: HPE's acquisition of Juniper closed in mid-2025, and pages now brand as 'HPE Juniper Networking.' The certification program continues unchanged so far, but it's fair to watch for program shifts — one more reason JNCIA works better as part of a multi-vendor foundation than as a single-track bet.

faq.question: Does JNCIA-Junos expire?
faq.answer: Valid for three years. Most people never re-take it — passing any higher-level Juniper exam (like a JNCIS) automatically renews everything beneath it, including your associate certs in other Juniper tracks. No annual fees, no CE-credit paperwork.

faq.question: What comes after JNCIA-Junos?
faq.answer: It's the shared gateway to Juniper's specialist tier: JNCIS-ENT (enterprise routing & switching), JNCIS-SP (service provider), and the security, data center, and automation tracks — then JNCIP and ultimately the JNCIE lab exams. If you're following the route/switch road, JNCIS-ENT is the natural next rung.
